title: Indian Diaspora Protests Outside India House in London Over NEET Controversy and Delhi Crackdown
excerpt: Demonstrators demanded Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET examination scandal and voiced solidarity with climate activist Sonam Wangchuk.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian diaspora protested in London, demanding Education Minister Pradhan's resignation over NEET controversy.
  • Demonstrators showed support for climate activist Sonam Wangchuk amid concerns over Delhi's political crackdowns.
  • Protesters chanted slogans and planned a follow-up demonstration in Leeds on July 26.
  • The protest highlights increasing political engagement of the Indian diaspora with domestic issues.

Protest details and context from the article.
  • Indian diaspora members protested outside India House in London, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET examination controversy
  • Protesters also expressed solidarity with Ladakh climate activist Sonam Wangchuk and raised concerns about political crackdowns in Delhi
  • Demonstrators chanted "Inquilab Zindabad" and "Pradhan Istifa Do" (Pradhan resign), with organisers scheduling a follow-up demonstration in Leeds on July 26
  • The protest reflects a growing trend of diaspora political engagement with domestic Indian issues

Members of the Indian diaspora in London staged a protest outside India House, the Indian High Commission, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the ongoing NEET (National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test) examination controversy that has roiled India's medical education system.

The Demands

Protesters carried placards and chanted slogans including "Inquilab Zindabad" (Long live the revolution) and "Pradhan Istifa Do" (Pradhan resign), echoing the language of student protests that have erupted across Indian university campuses in recent months.

The NEET controversy centres on allegations of question paper leaks, irregularities in scoring, and systemic corruption in the examination process that determines admission to India's medical colleges. The scandal has affected millions of aspiring doctors and their families, many of whom have diaspora connections in the UK, US, and Gulf countries.

Beyond the NEET issue, demonstrators also voiced solidarity with Sonam Wangchuk, the Ladakh-based climate activist and education reformer — the inspiration behind the film 3 Idiots — who has faced restrictions on his protest activities in Delhi. Wangchuk has been leading a campaign for Ladakh's inclusion under the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, which would provide greater autonomy and environmental protections for the region.

Diaspora Political Engagement

The London protest is part of a broader pattern of Indian diaspora communities becoming more vocal about domestic Indian political issues. In recent years, protests related to the Citizenship Amendment Act, farm laws, and now NEET have taken place outside Indian diplomatic missions in London, Washington, Toronto, and Sydney.

Organisers of the London demonstration announced plans for a follow-up protest in Leeds on July 26, suggesting the movement has legs beyond a one-off demonstration.

A Delicate Balance

For the Indian diaspora in the UK — estimated at over 1.8 million people and one of the country's largest ethnic minority groups — public protests against the Indian government's domestic policies remain a sensitive subject. Many diaspora members maintain deep ties to India while navigating their dual identity, and political engagement with Indian issues can create tensions within community organisations and with the Indian High Commission.

The NEET controversy, however, cuts across political lines. The examination affects families across the economic and political spectrum, making it a rare issue that unites diaspora members who might otherwise disagree on Indian domestic politics.
